# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Review of Varga & Holm, "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem"

Most of the forensic work in this comment is valuable. The attrition finding is new and important, and the record-vs-manager comparison and the actual-hours correction are exactly the analyses the Halden paper needed. The revenue and sectoral sections match concerns raised about the original working paper.

The comment's headline conclusion, however, does not follow from its own evidence. The gains are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty", it says, for reduced-hours schemes generally. Its corrections leave a positive residual. The randomised trial it calls the most reliable evidence also found per-hour gains. And the novelty argument is the weakest part of the paper.

## Arithmetic check

Most figures are consistent:
- **Table 2:** 95.1/0.800 = +18.9%; 98.4/0.859 = +14.6%; 95.4/0.861 = +10.8%.
- **Hours:** 40.3→34.6 is −14.1%; 40.4→34.8 is −13.9%.
- **Real revenue:** 1.014/1.041 = 0.974, a fall of 2.6%.

Two figures don't reconcile:

1. **The hours decomposition doesn't add up.** Section 3 attributes the gap to +0.7 hours per day on the four remaining days (2.8 h) and 1.6 h logged on the day off. That is 4.4 hours a week above the 32-hour schedule, implying about **36.4 hours**, not the reported 34.6. Either a component is misdescribed (for example, the +0.7 is measured against something other than the 8-hour scheduled day), or average actual hours are higher than reported. If the latter, the hours ratio is about 0.90 rather than 0.86, and the corrected per-hour gain is smaller still. This needs resolving, because Table 2 depends on it.
2. **The novelty extrapolation is miscalculated.** Energy fell from 0.61 SD to 0.29 SD between months three and six, about 0.107 SD per month. On a linear extrapolation it would reach baseline at about **month 8.7**, not "around month ten". This matters less than the problems with the extrapolation itself (see §3 below).

## 1. The conclusion contradicts the paper's own evidence

- **The comment's own correction leaves a positive gain.** After correcting output and hours, it still finds +10.8% per actual hour. Attributing that residual to novelty is a hypothesis, not a correction (see §3). The evidence shows a gain about half the reported size, not one that is entirely artifactual.
- **The randomised trial the comment praises found per-hour gains.** It calls the Varden counter-stratum result "the most reliable finding in the literature to date". But the same trial, using record-based output, timesheet hours and random assignment, also found **+12.5% output per actual hour in case-processing offices** (CI +6.9 to +18.4). That design addresses all three of the comment's concerns: measurement, selection, and the hours denominator. The comment cites only the stratum that fits its conclusion.
- **The scope of the claim is too broad.** The data note says correctly that the estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole". The abstract and conclusion then generalise to "reduced-hours schemes" in general. A re-analysis of one uncontrolled pilot can't establish that.

A conclusion the evidence supports would be closer to this:

> The Halden pilot overstated the per-hour gain by roughly half. Where output and hours can be measured properly, a gain of around 10% remains among surviving organisations. Whether it persists is unknown. In coverage-bound work, output per employee falls.

## 2. Attrition is described as corrected, but it isn't

The abstract says "Correcting the first three" of four problems, and attrition is listed first. But Table 2 corrects only output and hours. All 17 organisations in the final row are survivors, as §6 itself acknowledges ("in the subset of survivors").

The attrition finding is the comment's most important new fact. Seven of nine withdrawals came after the reduced schedule began, contradicting the working paper's account. But its effect on the estimate is not quantified. Possible analyses:
- **Bounding.** Assign the withdrawn organisations a range of plausible outcomes, from no change down to a large output loss. Report the pooled estimate under each, weighted by their staff numbers.
- **Partial data.** If the withdrawn organisations submitted any monthly indices before leaving, use them.
- **Describe the withdrawers.** Give their sectors and sizes. Six of the nine cited workload, so it matters whether they were concentrated in customer-facing sectors.

One minor point: six cited workload and two scheduling, which accounts for eight of the nine. The ninth reason isn't stated.

## 3. The novelty argument is speculation, and the data to test it are available

- **The extrapolation rests on too little.** The energy series has three points: 0 at baseline, 0.61 at month three, 0.29 at month six. It is non-monotonic. Drawing a straight line through the last two points assumes the conclusion, when the series could equally be plateauing.
- **Energy is not output.** Self-reported energy declining does not show that output per hour declined.
- **The obvious test isn't done.** The Halden output index was collected **monthly**, and the comment has the microdata. If the residual gain is novelty, output per hour should be falling across months two to six in the 17-organisation subset. The comment should report that trajectory. It is the most informative analysis available on the novelty question, and its absence is the comment's largest gap.
- **The burden of proof is shifted.** "The burden of proof lies with those claiming [durability]" is a fair argument against asserting a durable effect. It does not license asserting the opposite, that the effect is entirely novelty.

## 4. The meetings critique mischaracterises the Varden analysis

- **The offices were not "selected for analysis after the results were known".** The seven offices are all the treated case-processing offices in the trial. The calendar data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results.
- **The Varden authors were already cautious.** They said explicitly that the analysis was unregistered, that seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism", and that they had registered a confirmatory test. The comment's warning against citing it as a mechanism repeats what the original authors said.
- **The meetings hypothesis is a competing explanation the comment needs to answer.** If the gain comes from removing low-value standing meetings, it is a structural change, and there is no particular reason it would fade as novelty wears off. A fair treatment would say the residual is consistent with both novelty and process change, and that the two predict different trajectories.

## 5. Record-based output is better, but not neutral

The 19-of-23 pattern is convincing evidence that manager ratings run high. But "record-based" covers measures of very different validity:
- **Billable hours delivered is largely an input measure.** If billable hours fall with total hours, the record-based index measures time, not output. Output per hour then becomes a utilisation ratio. The comment should say how many of the 23 organisations used billable hours, and show results with and without them.
- **Measures like tickets closed and units produced** leave out quality and case mix, which is the same problem raised about the Varden case counts.
- **Report the 17-organisation subset as a baseline row in Table 2.** The rows use different samples (61, 23, 27, 17). Adding manager-reported output over scheduled hours for those 17 would separate the effect of the corrections from the effect of the subset. The 23-organisation subset's manager index (98.9) is close to the full sample's (98.7), which is reassuring.

## 6. Smaller points

- **No uncertainty is reported.** With 17 to 27 organisations, the corrected estimates need confidence intervals. The 11.2% fall for retail and hospitality rests on **three** organisations, and should be flagged as such.
- **Deflator.** CPI is a rough deflator for business revenue. Sector-specific price indices would be better, though the direction of the correction is probably right.
- **Wording.** "The hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points" is accurate (20% vs 14%) but only if the decomposition issue in the arithmetic check is resolved.

## Overall

Sections 1–5 are a useful correction to the Halden working paper. The attrition evidence is new and the measurement corrections are well executed, subject to the hours inconsistency. The comment would be stronger if it:

1. resolved the hours decomposition;
2. quantified attrition with bounds rather than counting it as corrected;
3. tested novelty using the monthly output series instead of extrapolating energy scores;
4. engaged with the Varden case-processing result;
5. replaced "entirely an artifact" with a conclusion matching its own estimate: the gain was roughly halved, and its durability is unknown.

As written, the comment criticises the Halden paper for drawing conclusions its data don't support, and then does the same.
